clinicalPearls: SPG37 is an autosomal dominant, pure (uncomplicated) hereditary spastic paraplegia defined by linkage to a locus on chromosome 8 (8p21.1-q13.3); the causative gene has not yet been identified, so the label rests on a compatible dominant pedigree after exclusion of known genes.

It presents with the core HSP picture: insidiously progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, extensor plantar responses, and spasticity that typically outstrips the degree of weakness.
Age at onset is variable, spanning childhood to adulthood, in keeping with a pure autosomal dominant HSP and with intrafamilial variability.
Because it is a pure form, cognition, speech, upper limbs, swallowing and vision are essentially spared; conspicuous extra-motor features should prompt reconsideration of a complicated subtype.
Urinary urgency and mild dorsal-column sensory blunting (reduced vibration sense at the toes) may accompany the gait disorder, as in other pure HSPs.
No molecular test is available for SPG37, so it is a diagnosis of exclusion reached only after common dominant genes (notably SPAST/SPG4 and ATL1/SPG3A) are negative.
There is no disease-modifying therapy; management is symptomatic, centred on spasticity control, physiotherapy, gait aids and bladder care.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG37 is an autosomal dominant, uncomplicated hereditary spastic paraplegia defined by genetic linkage to a locus on the proximal short and long arms of chromosome 8 (8p21.1-q13.3); unlike most characterised HSPs the specific causative gene has not been cloned, so its molecular basis is inferred rather than proven. As in the wider HSP group, the presumed pathology is a length-dependent, dying-back distal axonopathy of the longest descending corticospinal tract fibres and, to a lesser degree, ascending dorsal-column fibres, producing a central motor conduction defect that predominates in the legs. Candidate mechanisms shared across dominant pure HSP loci include disturbed axonal transport, abnormal endoplasmic-reticulum and organelle shaping, and defective membrane trafficking and mitochondrial distribution within long axons, but until the SPG37 gene is identified the precise pathway and the nature of any dominant-negative or haploinsufficiency effect remain speculative.
additionalDifferentials: SPG4 (SPAST) - the commonest autosomal dominant pure HSP and the principal mimic
SPG3A (ATL1) - typically early-onset autosomal dominant pure HSP
SPG6 (NIPA1), SPG8 (WASHC5) and SPG10 (KIF5A) - other autosomal dominant uncomplicated HSPs
SPG31 (REEP1) - autosomal dominant HSP with variable onset
Primary lateral sclerosis and early amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Compressive or structural myelopathy and dopa-responsive dystonia as treatable mimics of slowly progressive leg spasticity
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and whole spine to exclude structural, demyelinating or compressive myelopathy (usually normal or nonspecific in pure HSP)
Targeted HSP gene panel or exome sequencing to exclude known dominant genes such as SPAST and ATL1
Detailed three-generation family history, with linkage analysis to the 8p21-q13 region in sufficiently informative families
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to exclude peripheral neuropathy and motor neurone disease
Acquired-myelopathy screen (vitamin B12, copper, very-long-chain fatty acids and relevant serology)
Somatosensory and motor evoked potentials, which may show central conduction delay to the legs
redFlags: Prominent cognitive decline, seizures, ataxia, amyotrophy or optic involvement - point to a complicated HSP rather than SPG37
Rapidly progressive or markedly asymmetric weakness - reconsider motor neurone disease or a compressive lesion
A sensory level, disproportionate sphincter failure or back pain - mandate cord imaging for a structural cause
Bulbar or upper-limb onset - atypical for a pure lower-limb HSP
reference.prognosis: As a pure autosomal dominant HSP, SPG37 is generally slowly progressive with a normal life expectancy; many affected individuals retain independent or aided walking for decades, although gait disability tends to accrue gradually over time.
pitfalls: Labelling a family as SPG37 without first excluding the common dominant genes, especially SPAST - it is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Assuming the gene is known and attempting to order a specific SPG37 gene test, when no such molecular test exists.
Attributing any complicating feature to SPG37 instead of revisiting the diagnosis.
Overlooking a treatable acquired myelopathy that can masquerade as slowly progressive HSP.
